title: OpenAI shares its internal progress numbers and asks AI labs to agree limits. AI stocks end their worst week in years, Together AI says a coding agent leaked a key to stored prompts, and the best agents finish under 8% of tasks in a pretend company. US governors and South Korea set out new AI rules.
summary: OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published internal perplexity figures, from about 0.99 for GPT-3.5 to below 0.8 today, and proposed common limits labs would not cross until AI monitoring improves; Sam Altman backs it. The Nasdaq fell 10% last week and Nvidia 14% on Friday; US futures rose on Sunday while Korea’s Kospi fell on Monday. Together AI says an AI coding agent committed a credential that let an outsider download stored prompts from June and July. In the SWE-CoWork test, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra completed under 8% of assignments that required working with simulated colleagues. US governors asked Congress for national AI rules that leave states room to protect workers, and South Korea published draft rules for training AI on personal data.
uncertainty: OpenAI’s perplexity figures come from its own internal codebase dataset and cannot be compared with other labs; no other lab has agreed to the proposal. Market figures are as of CNBC’s updates and will move. Together’s review of the leaked prompts is still under way. SWE-CoWork is one research group’s benchmark, not yet peer reviewed. The governors’ principles and Korea’s draft rules are not law yet.

stories.theme: OpenAI’s chief scientist publishes its internal progress numbers and asks AI labs to agree limits they will not cross until safety tools catch up
stories.changed: On 22 November 2026 OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published “Perplexity and Intelligence”, and Sam Altman called it “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile”. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next piece of text; lower is better. For the first time OpenAI shared its own internal figures, measured on a held-out sample of its codebase: about 0.99 for GPT-3.5, about 0.91 for GPT-4, and below 0.8 for today’s models, which is where Pachocki says strong abilities in cybersecurity and mathematics appeared. He says a model at about 0.76 started producing major maths results, and expects more “transformative capabilities” in a window of about 0.68 to 0.7. He proposes that labs agree common limits, based on perplexity and other measures, that they will not cross until tools for understanding and monitoring AI reach a concrete milestone. He also warns that AI could speed up its own training research “as soon as 2027”. Reuters reports Altman backs the proposal.
stories.matters: A leading lab is asking rivals to pause at an agreed point rather than race. If labs adopt it, the pace of new models, and of the tools built on them, could become more predictable.
stories.imply: This is a proposal, not a rule, and no other lab has signed up. Pachocki lists the weak spots himself: labs measure on different data, the number does not track real tasks, and reasoning gains do not show up in it.
uses: When you plan AI projects a year out, assume new abilities can arrive suddenly rather than in steady steps.
Ask your AI vendors how they test new models for safety before release, and what they would do if a limit like this were agreed.
Watch for shared industry standards on testing; they are likely to end up in procurement checklists.
stories.example: A head of risk adds a line to the firm’s AI policy: before switching to any new frontier model, the team reads the vendor’s safety report and runs its own tests on a sample of real work.
stories.audience: Leaders setting AI strategy, risk and compliance teams, and anyone who buys AI services.
stories.watch: Whether Anthropic, Google or others respond or publish their own figures, and whether the White House Accords that Altman mentions take the idea up.

source.title: OpenAI (Jakub Pachocki): Perplexity and Intelligence, 22 November 2026
source.quote: I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone

stories.theme: AI stocks had their worst week in years; US futures bounced on Sunday, but Asian AI chip makers kept falling on Monday
stories.changed: US stocks ended last week in what traders call correction territory, more than 10% below their records, with worries about AI driving the fall. CNBC says the Nasdaq Composite fell 10% for the week, its worst since March 2020, and is now down for 2026. Nvidia fell 14% on Friday after Reuters reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into its accounting; it is down nearly 40% in November. Anthropic, which listed on Thursday at $83 a share and traded above $115, closed the week at $88.91. CNBC also points to fears that AI growth is slowing and to higher interest rates. On Sunday evening US time, S&P 500 futures rose 2.03% and Nasdaq-100 futures 2.76%. In Asia on Monday, South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.16%, with Samsung Electronics down about 3.6% and SK Hynix 3.2%, at the time of CNBC’s update. Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell, down 25% and 34% this month, report results on Monday and Tuesday.
stories.matters: Share prices pay for data centres, chips and start-up salaries. A long slide can mean tighter AI budgets, fewer free tiers and more pressure on vendors to show real revenue.
stories.imply: Prices move faster than products. Nothing about the AI tools you use changed this week, but vendor finances, discounts and roadmaps may, especially for smaller suppliers that depend on new funding.
uses: Check which AI suppliers you depend on are young firms that need fresh funding, and keep an export of your data.
Push for longer price locks or credits in AI contracts while vendors want to show steady sales.
If your team’s budget assumes AI cost cuts, write down what happens if prices rise instead.
stories.example: An operations manager renewing an AI transcription tool asks for a two-year price lock and a clause to export all recordings if the supplier is sold or shuts down.
stories.audience: Finance teams, procurement, founders raising money and anyone with AI suppliers on contract.
stories.watch: HPE and Dell results this week, the US Thanksgiving-shortened trading days, and any more news on the SEC look at Nvidia.

source.quote: U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory.

stories.theme: Together AI says an AI coding agent leaked a key, and an outsider used it to download stored customer prompts
stories.changed: On 21 November 2026 Together AI, a company that runs open models for other businesses, told customers that an unauthorised party downloaded samples of prompts sent to its service in June and July. The company had kept the samples for software testing in a private Hugging Face repository. While working on Together’s public GitHub project xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that opened that private store. Together’s scanning caught it and the change was reversed, but the key had already been taken. The party then searched the prompts for passwords and keys to other services and tried them; five of those were decoy credentials planted in a Dragos security experiment. The prompts went to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 models, mostly on 24 June and 4, 8 and 14 July. Together says it is still reviewing what was exposed, has made zero data retention the default for new accounts, now checks every pull request for credentials and has changed its rules for AI coding agents.
stories.matters: Two lessons in one incident: AI providers may keep copies of your prompts, and AI coding agents can leak secrets in seconds. Existing accounts do not get the new zero-retention default.
stories.imply: Anything typed into an AI service can outlive the conversation. Treat prompts like email: do not include passwords or keys, and check each provider’s retention setting yourself.
uses: If you used those three models through Together in June or July, change any password or key that appeared in a prompt.
Turn on zero data retention in every AI provider account where it exists, including older accounts.
Add automatic secret scanning to repositories where AI coding agents commit code.
stories.example: A developer whose support bot sent customer tickets through Together in July changes the API keys that appeared in those tickets, then switches on zero data retention in the account settings.
stories.audience: Developers, security teams and anyone who sends business data to AI providers through an API.
stories.watch: Direct notices from Together to affected customers, what its review finds in the prompts, and whether other providers change their retention defaults.

source.title: Together AI (Vipul Ved Prakash): Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026, 21 November 2026
source.quote: During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository.

stories.theme: Put inside a pretend software company, the best AI coding agents finished fewer than 8% of assignments
stories.changed: A new test called SWE-CoWork, reported by The Decoder on 22 November 2026, treats AI coding agents like new hires. Each of 101 assignments, taken from 101 real code projects, starts with a brief handoff note. The agent has to find out what to build from 26 simulated colleagues, a project board and chat history, sort out conflicting information, then write and check the code. The two best models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, passed about 63% of the tests for new features but fully completed only 6.93% and 7.92% of assignments. Giving them the full requirements upfront raised the share of passed tests by about 16 percentage points for two models but did not raise full completions. Claude Opus 5.5 sent 93% of its first questions to the right colleague but still obtained only 64% of the requirements colleagues held. The researchers say agents let follow-up questions drop, and 31% of the requirements agents reported as done failed their tests.
stories.matters: Agents can write code well but struggle with the parts of a job that involve people: chasing answers, following up and checking work before saying it is done.
stories.imply: Clear written specs help but are not enough. Teams that hand work to agents still need someone to own the requirements and to check “done” against tests, not the agent’s own report.
uses: Give agents a written checklist of requirements and ask them to tick each one against a test.
Do not accept an agent’s “completed” message; run the tests or review the change yourself.
Keep a person in charge of chasing open questions with colleagues when an agent is working on a team task.
stories.example: A team lead hands a bug fix to a coding agent with a list of five acceptance tests, and merges only after all five pass in the pipeline, whatever the agent’s summary says.
stories.audience: Engineering managers, developers using coding agents and anyone planning to give agents team work.
stories.watch: Whether other labs run their models on the test, and whether new agent features target follow-up and checking rather than raw coding.

source.title: arXiv (TokenWave AI): SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations; reported by The Decoder, 22 November 2026
source.quote: The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments.

stories.theme: US governors from both parties ask Washington for national AI rules, while keeping states in charge of protecting workers, consumers and children
stories.changed: On 22 November 2026 the National Governors Association published principles for governing AI, from a bipartisan council led by Maryland’s Wes Moore, Indiana’s Mike Braun, North Carolina’s Josh Stein and Utah’s Spencer Cox. They say the federal government should handle national and international risks as AI is developed, while states keep the flexibility to protect people and govern how AI is used. Bloomberg reports the plan calls for independent safety reviews of advanced models and for developers to report serious security breaches and safety incidents. The principles also say job creation should be a core priority, that workers need protection and support through change, that rules should match evidence-based risks, and that laws should not favour big companies over small ones. They are meant to inform the incoming Congress.
stories.matters: The fight over whether Washington should override state AI laws is shaping what US employers must do. Governors from both parties now want a national framework but not one that wipes out state rules.
stories.imply: Expect two layers of rules in the US: federal duties for the biggest model makers and state duties for companies that use AI with workers and customers.
uses: Keep a simple list of where your company uses AI in hiring, pay or customer decisions; state rules focus there.
Track the state AI laws that apply where you have staff or customers, not only federal news.
Ask AI vendors how they would report a serious security or safety incident to you.
stories.example: An HR director with staff in five US states keeps a one-page register of every AI tool used in hiring and reviews, ready for whichever state rules apply.
stories.audience: HR, legal and compliance teams at US employers, and AI vendors selling to them.
stories.watch: Bills in the new Congress, whether they include the governors’ split of duties, and how the White House responds.

source.title: National Governors Association: Governors Call for AI Action, 22 November 2026
source.quote: We agree that humans must stay in control, and we must protect our people – especially workers, consumers and our kids.

stories.theme: South Korea drafts the rules for using personal data to build AI: a named person in charge, access controls and risk checks
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission opened public comment, until 4 January 2027, on the detailed rules for its new “AI exception”. A revised law lets organisations use personal data they collected lawfully to develop AI, after the commission approves it, when anonymised or pseudonymised data is not enough and the project has a public and social benefit. The draft says organisations using the exception must appoint a person in charge and keep an internal management plan, stay within what was approved, restrict who can access the data and destroy it when it is no longer needed. Higher-risk projects need a risk assessment first, for example when they use sensitive data or ID numbers, involve children, track or predict people’s behaviour, or make decisions that significantly affect people’s rights. Similar cases can get a faster review, and an expert committee will be set up. The rules are due to take effect with the law on 9 March 2027.
stories.matters: It is one of the clearest sets of rules yet on when a company may train AI on customer data, and what it must do in return. Other regulators often borrow such templates.
stories.imply: Using customer data for AI is moving from a legal grey area to a permission with paperwork: an owner, a scope, access limits and a deletion date.
uses: If you build AI with Korean customers’ data, name an owner and write down the scope before March 2027.
Check whether anonymised data would be enough; the exception only applies when it is not.
Use the draft as a checklist for any internal AI project that touches personal data, wherever you are.
stories.example: A retailer with Korean shoppers plans a recommendation model, names a data owner, limits access to three engineers and sets a date to delete the training copy after launch.
stories.audience: Data, privacy and legal teams at companies with users in South Korea, and AI teams anywhere working with customer data.
stories.watch: Comments submitted by 4 January, the final text, and the first projects the commission approves.

source.title: The Asia Business Daily: Use of Personal Information for AI Development to Require Appointment of Person in Charge, Access Controls, 23 November 2026
source.quote: In cases involving a significant risk of personal information infringement, organizations will be required to conduct a “risk factor assessment” in advance.
